From Signals to Evidence: Interpretable Underwater Acoustic Target Sensing
with Large Language Models
— Part I: Framework and RecognitionThanks: Corresponding author: Jie Chen. Y. Zhang, J. Chen, Z. Zhao, X. Yang, J.-D. Yuge Zhang    Jie Chen    Zhengqiao Zhao    Xiling Yao Affiliation: Lingji Xu, Jingdong Chen, Yixin Yang
Abstract

Underwater acoustic target detection and recognition are essential to marine surveillance and intelligent ocean sensing. Despite substantial advances in deep learning, existing systems typically produce binary detection decisions, categorical labels, or scalar confidence scores, offering limited insight into the physical evidence underlying their outputs. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) present an opportunity to move underwater acoustic sensing toward interpretable, evidence-grounded understanding. However, generic audio encoders often fail to capture the distinctive physical characteristics of underwater acoustics, while the scarcity of physically annotated data remains a major obstacle. In this paper, the first of a two-part series, we propose a from-signals-to-evidence framework that integrates physics-aware acoustic encoding with a pretrained LLM. The framework is built around a unified feature–evidence–decision chain and a shared reasoning core. Its open, extensible input layer accommodates heterogeneous information, including raw waveforms, time–frequency representations, environmental and geographic data, and textual physical priors, enabling detection and recognition to be formulated within a common framework. In Part I, we instantiate this framework for target recognition through an Underwater Acoustic Physics-aware Transformer (UPT), which tokenizes complementary acoustic representations and learns task-disentangled physical representations through four physics-oriented learning tasks. To support this process, we develop a physics-parameterized data engine that provides traceable supervision at two levels of granularity and introduce an attribute-level evaluation protocol to assess the physical fidelity of generated descriptions. Experiments on simulated recordings of four vessels demonstrate accurate vessel recognition and reliable estimation of shaft frequency, blade-passing frequency, and machinery-related attributes. These results establish the feasibility of evidence-grounded underwater acoustic recognition and lay the foundation for Part II, which extends the framework to target detection under low signal-to-noise ratio conditions.

Index Terms: 
Underwater acoustic target recognition, Interpretable recognition, Large language models, Physics-aware acoustic encoding, Physics-based acoustic simulation, Evidence-grounded description

I Introduction

Passive underwater acoustic sensing forms a cornerstone of marine surveillance, maritime traffic safety, and intelligent ocean observation [1, 2]. Its processing chain consists of two main stages: detection and recognition. Detection determines whether a target is present in the received acoustic field, often under low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) conditions. Recognition then identifies the target by analyzing faint, structured acoustic signatures in ship-radiated noise, including tonal lines, envelope modulations, and machinery-related spectral components [3, 4]. The two stages are intimately coupled: detection acts as the front-end gatekeeper, close to the raw acoustic field where signatures are weakest, while recognition operates downstream on detected contacts. These signatures are severely attenuated and distorted during propagation, while different vessel categories can exhibit similar spectral and modulation patterns. These factors make reliable detection and robust recognition long-standing challenges in underwater acoustics [5, 1]. Interpretability is becoming increasingly important throughout this processing chain. Operators and autonomous systems need to understand not only the system’s decisions but also the physical evidence underlying them. However, both detection and recognition remain largely reliant on methods that offer limited insight into their decision-making processes.

Both detection and recognition have evolved through two broad generations of methods. Early approaches relied on handcrafted acoustic features, including tonal features extracted through low-frequency analysis and recording (LOFAR), modulation spectra obtained through detection of envelope modulation on noise (DEMON), and Mel-frequency cepstral coefficients (MFCCs), combined with shallow classifiers for recognition [6, 1], while detection typically employed energy detectors or, when suitable signal templates were available, matched filters [7]. Although these methods offered a degree of physical interpretability, their performance was often limited in complex acoustic environments. The advent of deep neural networks marked a significant advance, improving recognition accuracy and detection capability by learning discriminative representations directly from time–frequency data [8, 9, 10]. Yet, despite these advances, the underlying decision paradigm has remained largely opaque. Modern systems typically accompany a detection decision or recognition label with a confidence score. Such scores indicate the system’s degree of certainty but offer little insight into the acoustic evidence that supports its conclusion. Moreover, confidence estimates may be poorly calibrated [11] and do not reveal how individual acoustic cues contribute to a decision. Addressing this limitation requires more than improving predictive accuracy; it calls for a fundamental shift in how sensing decisions are formulated and presented. The goal is to move beyond hard labels and scalar confidence scores toward evidence-grounded decisions that explain not only what the system concludes, but also which physical signatures support that conclusion. This capability is critical to establishing calibrated human trust and enabling machine-to-machine verification in distributed sensing systems [12, 13].

Building on this vision, we propose an Underwater acoustic Physics-aware Description (UPD) framework, a unified detection-and-recognition framework that couples a physics-aware acoustic encoder with a pretrained LLM through cross-modal alignment, as illustrated in Fig. 1. The framework is organized around an ordered feature–evidence–decision chain: raw observations are first transformed into physically meaningful tokens anchored to identifiable acoustic structures (tonal lines, envelope modulations, machinery components), the shared LLM reasoning core then identifies and states the acoustic evidence bearing on the problem in light of textual physical priors, and final judgments are produced conditioned on the stated evidence rather than directly on the features, distinguishing the framework from post-hoc explanation schemes. Its input layer is deliberately open: representative inputs include, but are not limited to, waveform-level observations from single or multiple hydrophones possibly behind physical front ends such as beamforming, general and physics-informed time–frequency imagery, environmental and geographic information as imagery or structured parameters, and textual physical priors, and new sources are incorporated simply by adding encoders or extending the textual context, without architectural modification. Detection and recognition are two instantiations of the same chain, sharing the semantic core while differing in operating conditions, input nature, depth of the physical front end, and the role of the environment. In the present Part I, we instantiate this general framework for recognition: the encoder performs disentangled representation learning over four physics-oriented acoustic tasks, tokenizing complementary time–frequency representations, e.g., Mel spectrograms, time-varying line spectra, and DEMON spectra, into physically meaningful units; the aligned LLM generates a structured description covering vessel identity, operating state, shaft-frequency range and its temporal trend, blade-passing frequency, machinery-related spectral lines, and the observation conditions, together with the acoustic evidence on which these judgments rest. To overcome data scarcity, we further develop a physics-based simulation pipeline that synthesizes vessel-radiated noise with fully known source and channel parameters, from which dual-granularity supervision—discrete physical attribute labels and structured textual descriptions—is derived.

Given this generality, the two instantiations are developed in two companion papers, following the detection–recognition chain in the direction of increasing signal-condition difficulty.

Part I, the present paper, establishes the framework and validates it through the recognition instantiation described above, which operates on detected, preprocessed contacts where signal conditions and physical priors are comparatively well defined—offering the most direct demonstration of the proposed paradigm.

Part II advances upstream to the detection instantiation under low-SNR conditions, which operates closer to the raw acoustic field and demands a deeper integration of propagation physics into the framework.

The main contributions of the present paper (Part I) are summarized as follows:

  • •

    We propose a physics-aware underwater acoustic detection-and-recognition framework that, to our knowledge, is the first to couple a physics-oriented acoustic encoder with an LLM to produce structured, evidence-bearing descriptions of vessel-radiated noise; its Part I instantiation targets recognition, advancing it from hard labels toward interpretable decisions.

  • •

    We design an underwater acoustic physics-aware transformer that tokenizes complementary acoustic representations and learns task-disentangled physical representations through four physics-oriented tasks, endowing acoustic tokens with explicit physical meaning.

  • •

    We develop a physics-based simulation pipeline with dual-granularity supervision, pairing each synthesized signal with discrete physical attribute labels and structured textual descriptions, enabling physically grounded training and field-wise evaluation.

  • •

    Extensive experiments on simulated data of four vessels demonstrate accurate vessel recognition alongside reliable estimation of shaft-frequency, blade-passing, and machinery-related physical attributes, validating the feasibility of evidence-grounded underwater acoustic recognition.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews related work. Section 3 presents the UPD framework. Section 4 describes the physics-based data construction. Section 5 reports experimental results, followed by discussion in Section 6 and conclusions in Section 7.

II Related Work

II-A Underwater Acoustic Target Recognition

Underwater acoustic target recognition has long relied on handcrafted representations of ship-radiated noise. Classical acoustic analysis methods extract characteristic spectral and modulation patterns from received signals. Representative techniques include LOFAR, which reveals narrowband tonal structures [14], and DEMON, which extracts modulation components associated with propeller rotation [3]. The resulting shaft-frequency lines, blade-rate harmonics, and machinery-related components provide physically meaningful cues for identifying targets and interpreting their operating states. Other feature-based approaches use Mel-frequency cepstral coefficients (MFCCs) to summarize spectral characteristics and combine them with statistical classifiers such as Gaussian mixture models [15]. These methods separate expert-designed feature extraction from the subsequent recognition stage. However, extracting stable features remains challenging when weak tonal components are obscured by noise or when signal characteristics vary over time. Their dependence on expert-defined features also limits scalability and adaptability to unfamiliar targets and operating conditions.

The past decade has witnessed a shift toward data-driven approaches. Convolutional and recurrent neural networks operating on time–frequency representations have substantially improved classification accuracy on public vessel-noise datasets such as ShipsEar and DeepShip [8, 9, 16]. Subsequent studies introduce attention mechanisms and residual architectures to emphasize informative features, as exemplified by the attention-based residual network of Li et al. [17]. Transformer-based models extend the modeling of dependencies across time–frequency tokens. MHT-UATR-Transformer [18] further combines hierarchical tokenization with masked reconstruction for self-supervised representation learning. Researchers have also explored data augmentation [8], transfer learning [17], and few-shot adaptation [19] to train recognition models with limited labeled data. Despite these advances in representation and learning, the output typically remains a categorical label, occasionally accompanied by a scalar confidence score. Such outputs state neither which acoustic structures support the decision nor how environmental factors have shaped the observation. Improved classification performance therefore does not, by itself, provide an explicit account of the physical evidence underlying recognition.

More recent studies incorporate physical characteristics or linguistic knowledge into the recognition process. Xie et al. propose DEMONet [20], which uses DEMON-derived characteristics to route signals among expert networks. In language-guided recognition, Xie et al. introduce UART [21], a tri-modal contrastive framework that aligns audio, spectrograms, and templated descriptions. Fu et al. develop MF-UATR [19], which combines pretrained language-audio representations with multi-feature contrastive learning. Cao et al. propose ASE-CLAP [22], which uses an LLM to construct acoustic-semantic descriptions and enrich class prototypes for similarity-based classification. These methods demonstrate the value of physical and semantic information, but the decision paradigm has remained essentially unchanged: such information primarily improves category prediction, while the model does not generate a structured account of the acoustic evidence for each recording. This limits the basis for human assessment or machine-to-machine verification in operational and distributed sensing scenarios. Advancing underwater acoustic recognition therefore requires upgrading the form of the decision itself—from labels and scores to structured, evidence-bearing descriptions—and that this upgrade calls for modeling capabilities beyond conventional classifier architectures.

II-B Large Audio-Language Models and Cross-Modal Alignment

Large language models pretrained on massive text corpora have demonstrated strong sequence modeling, knowledge retention, and instruction-following capabilities. These capabilities have been extended to the audio modality through a series of audio-language and large audio-language models (LALMs) [23, 24, 25, 26]. A common architecture pairs a pretrained audio encoder [27, 28] with an LLM through a lightweight projection or alignment module, enabling audio-conditioned question answering and description generation. The encoder represents the acoustic observation, while the alignment module maps its outputs into embeddings that the language model can process alongside textual instructions. SALMONN [25], for example, connects complementary speech and general-audio encoders to an LLM through a window-level Q-Former. Qwen-Audio [24] supports a broad range of speech, music, and sound-understanding tasks, while Audio Flamingo [26] extends audio interaction to in-context learning and multi-turn dialogue. GAMA [29] further explores reasoning-oriented instruction tuning for complex audio understanding. These developments enable a single model to perform multiple audio-understanding tasks through natural-language instructions and generate descriptions of sound events and their acoustic characteristics.

Parameter-efficient fine-tuning reduces the computational cost of adapting pretrained models. LoRA [30], for example, keeps pretrained weights frozen and learns low-rank updates, reducing the number of trainable parameters and memory requirements. The availability of labeled data is another consideration in adapting pretrained models to specialized domains. Domain-specific systems such as LLaVA-Med [31] and GeoChat [32] adapt general vision-language models to biomedical imaging and remote sensing through domain alignment and instruction tuning. Their results suggest that pretrained knowledge and reasoning capabilities can be reused with targeted supervision, an attractive direction for underwater acoustics, where annotated recordings are scarce. However, generating a convincing explanation does not ensure that it reflects the evidence used to make a prediction [33, 34]. For underwater recognition, this motivates grounding generated descriptions in verifiable acoustic evidence.

In addition, existing general-purpose LALMs are primarily designed to understand speech, music, and environmental sounds, and their ability to recognize physically structured underwater signals remains uncertain. A concurrent benchmark, UA-Bench [35], evaluated nine open LALMs without task-specific adaptation on synthesized underwater acoustic signals. Under its gated coarse-to-fine evaluation protocol, the highest leaf-level accuracy was 13.1%, compared with a random reference of 7.7%. Four models showed reliable improvements in leaf-level accuracy over a paired silent-audio control, with a maximum improvement of 4.7 percentage points. These findings indicate limitations in the evaluated models’ transfer to fine-grained underwater recognition. They motivate exploring physics-aware adaptation to capture the underwater-specific physical characteristics on which vessel recognition depends. The present work develops such an adaptation framework: we couple a physics-oriented acoustic encoder with a pretrained LLM to produce fine-grained, evidence-bearing physical descriptions of vessel-radiated noise.

III From-Signals-to-Evidence Framework

Conventional underwater acoustic systems compress an observation into a decision, ,whether a detection flag or a class label, discarding the intermediate physical reasoning that a human expert would articulate. The proposed framework in contrast makes the intermediate reasoning explicit and organizes the entire processing pipeline around an ordered feature–evidence–decision chain, as illustrated in Fig. 2

ℱ=ϕ⁡(𝒳),ℰ=g⁡(ℱ,𝒫),𝒟=h⁡(ℰ),\mathcal{F}=\phi(\mathcal{X}),\qquad\mathcal{E}=g(\mathcal{F},\mathcal{P}),\qquad\mathcal{D}=h(\mathcal{E}), (1)

where 𝒳\mathcal{X} denotes the multimodal observations, 𝒫\mathcal{P} the textual physical priors, ϕ\phi the acoustic encoder, and gg, hh the evidence-forming and decision-making processes realized by the shared reasoning core. Raw observations are first transformed into physically meaningful representations (feature); the system then identifies and states the acoustic structures that bear on the problem at hand, in light of available physical priors (evidence); final judgments are produced conditioned on the stated evidence (decision). Notably, the decision 𝒟\mathcal{D} is conditioned on the evidence ℰ\mathcal{E} rather than directly on the features ℱ\mathcal{F}, which distinguishes this chain from post-hoc explanation schemes in which justifications are generated independently of the decision process.

Two further principles guide the design. First, physical grounding is maintained throughout the processing chain. Extracted features correspond to identifiable acoustic structures, such as tonal lines, envelope modulations, and machinery-related components, rather than opaque activations, allowing the resulting evidence to be verified against the input. Second, heterogeneous information is represented within a shared semantic space. Acoustic signals, time–frequency representations, and textual physical priors are mapped into the embedding space of a large language model (LLM), which serves as the unified reasoning core. Although the framework is instantiated differently for detection and recognition, both tasks follow the same feature–evidence–decision chain and share the same reasoning core.

III-A Multimodal Input Layer

The framework is designed to accommodate the heterogeneous information available in underwater sensing, without prescribing a closed set of input types. Representative inputs include, but are not limited to: (i) waveform-level observations, i.e., the received time series from single or multiple hydrophones, possibly preprocessed by a physical front end such as beamforming; (ii) time–frequency imagery, including general-purpose spectrograms and physics-informed representations such as time-varying line spectra and DEMON spectra, which render specific acoustic structures visually explicit; (iii) environmental and geographic information, such as sound speed profiles, bathymetric charts, sea state, and seabed properties, expressed either as imagery or as structured parameters; and (iv) textual physical priors and expert knowledge, expressed in natural language. Whereas conventional architectures can absorb such heterogeneous information only through ad-hoc feature engineering, the language-modeling interface allows imagery, parameters, and textual priors to be aligned into a unified semantic space and injected as context or instructions, without architectural modification. The input layer is thus extensible: new information sources can be incorporated by adding the corresponding encoders or simply by extending the textual context.

III-B Physics-Aware Acoustic Encoding

The acoustic encoder ϕ\phi in Eq. (1) maps observations to physically meaningful tokens, each associated with an identifiable acoustic structure, providing concrete referents for subsequent evidence statements. Its design follows three principles. First, complementary time–frequency representations are encoded through separate pathways rather than fused at an early stage, preserving the distinct physical characteristics of each representation. Second, the encoder is trained on physics-oriented analysis tasks, such as shaft-frequency and modulation analysis for recognition and coherent integration and bearing analysis for detection, rather than optimized solely for the final decision. This encourages the learned tokens to capture how a target sounds, rather than merely which label it belongs to. Third, conventional physical processing, including filtering, normalization, beamforming, and Doppler compensation, is retained as a parameterized front end wherever it incorporates established physical knowledge, with the learnable encoder built upon it. The extent of this physical integration depends on the task and constitutes a key architectural distinction between the detection and recognition instantiations (Section III-E).

III-C LLM Reasoning Core and Cross-Modal Alignment

All input modalities are organized into a single token sequence for the reasoning core,

𝐒=[ρ⁡(𝐙ac);ψ⁡(𝐈env);Emb⁡(𝐓)],\mathbf{S}=\big[\,\rho(\mathbf{Z}_{\mathrm{ac}});\ \psi(\mathbf{I}_{\mathrm{env}});\ \mathrm{Emb}(\mathbf{T})\,\big], (2)

where 𝐙ac\mathbf{Z}_{\mathrm{ac}} denotes acoustic tokens produced by the encoder, ρ⁡(⋅)\rho(\cdot) a lightweight acoustic projection, 𝐈env\mathbf{I}_{\mathrm{env}} environmental imagery with its encoder ψ\psi, and Emb⁡(𝐓)\mathrm{Emb}(\mathbf{T}) the embeddings of textual tokens including queries, instructions, and physical priors. The concatenated sequence 𝐒\mathbf{S} is processed by a LLM, which acts as the shared reasoning core: it aggregates evidence across representations and priors, and generates responses in an ordered evidence-then-decision manner. The pretrained parameters are kept frozen and adapted through low-rank modules, so that the pretrained knowledge and instruction-following capability are preserved while the learning burden is confined to the acoustic-to-semantic mapping. Training supervises only the answer portion of each sequence,

ℒ=−∑i∈𝒜logPθ(Ai|𝐒,A<i),\mathcal{L}=-\sum_{i\in\mathcal{A}}\log P_{\theta}\!\left(A_{i}\,\middle|\,\mathbf{S},A_{<i}\right), (3)

where 𝒜\mathcal{A} denotes the answer token positions, and losses over queries, instructions, and input portions are masked out. This design directs the learning signal toward evidence-based reasoning: extracting relevant evidence from acoustic features and using it to support subsequent decisions, rather than reproducing the input. By sharing a common reasoning core across tasks, the framework also provides a flexible query interface through which a single model addresses vessel identification, physical attribute estimation, and target detection, without relying on separate task-specific output heads.

III-D Evidence-Grounded Output

The output of the framework is a structured description rather than a bare decision. Formally, each response is organized as

𝒟=⟨d;e1,e2,…,eM⟩,em↔ℱm⊆ℱ,\mathcal{D}=\langle d;\ e_{1},e_{2},\dots,e_{M}\rangle,\qquad e_{m}\leftrightarrow\mathcal{F}_{m}\subseteq\mathcal{F}, (4)

where dd denotes the decision and each evidence item eme_{m} is linked to a verifiable subset ℱm\mathcal{F}_{m} of the acoustic features. Evidence statements may refer, for example, to tonal-line locations, modulation patterns, and estimated observation conditions, as well as to missing components that are attributable to the propagation environment rather than to the absence of the target. A fixed field order is imposed on the description, which enforces the evidence-then-decision ordering during generation, renders every attribute individually parseable for evaluation, and allows each reported statement to be independently verified against the input. In this sense, the framework replaces a single opaque score with an inspectable chain whose correctness can be checked link by link.

III-E A Unified View of Detection and Recognition

Detection and recognition have traditionally been addressed as separate problems using distinct architectures. Within the proposed framework, however, they are two instantiations of a common feature–evidence–decision chain, sharing the same semantic core but differing in four key respects. First, their operating conditions differ. Recognition typically operates on target-bearing segments, often identified through prior detection, where the signal-to-noise ratio is relatively favorable and the relevant physical priors are well established. Detection, by contrast, must operate on continuous observations in which the target, if present, may be deeply buried in noise.

Second, their input requirements differ. Recognition primarily processes single-channel, target-centered recordings, whereas detection must accommodate multichannel array signals over extended observation periods and provide spatial information, such as target bearing, alongside target-presence decisions.

Third, the extent of physical front-end integration differs. Detection relies more heavily on parameterized physical processing, including array processing, coherent integration, and Doppler compensation, applied before or within the encoder. Recognition, in contrast, places greater emphasis on learning representations of spectral and temporal structure.

Fourth, environmental information serves different purposes. In recognition, environmental priors help explain how propagation shapes the observed acoustic features. In detection, they also support predictive modeling of the noise field, fading, and channel-induced distortion. Anticipating these effects is important for identifying potential target signatures against background interference and improving bearing estimation.

This paper (Part I) establishes the framework and validates its recognition instantiation, where target-bearing recordings allow the relationship between acoustic features and physical attributes to be examined directly. Part II extends the framework to low-SNR detection, with particular emphasis on multichannel processing and environmental prediction.

IV Recognition Instantiation: Physics-Aware Encoding

In the remainder of this paper, we instantiate the framework of Section III for the recognition task. The instantiation follows the three encoding rules established in Section 3.3: complementary representations are tokenized independently (Section 4.1), the encoder is supervised by physics-oriented analysis tasks rather than vessel identity alone (Sections 4.2–4.3), and the resulting tokens are aligned with the reasoning core under an answer-only objective (Section 4.4). The resulting acoustic encoder is termed the Underwater acoustic Physics-aware Transformer (UPT), and the complete recognition system, which couples UPT with a pretrained LLM, is illustrated in Fig.3.

IV-A Complementary Representations and Independent Tokenization

IV-A1 Complementary acoustic representations.

Following the representation-diversity rule, three representations with distinct physical meanings and time–frequency resolutions are extracted from each received signal x⁡(t)x(t). The Log-Mel spectrogram captures the overall energy distribution,

Xmel=log⁡|STFT⁡{x⁡(t)}|2​Wmel,X_{\mathrm{mel}}=\log\left|\mathrm{STFT}\{x(t)\}\right|^{2}W_{\mathrm{mel}}, (5)

where WmelW_{\mathrm{mel}} denotes the Mel filterbank. To resolve narrowband rotating-machinery components, a time-varying line spectrum is computed from a resampled waveform using a long-window STFT,

Xline=log⁡|Xline​(τ,f)|2,X_{\mathrm{line}}=\log\left|X_{\mathrm{line}}(\tau,f)\right|^{2}, (6)

which preserves the trajectories of tonal components over time. The time-varying DEMON spectrogram characterizes the temporal evolution of low-frequency envelope modulation: after band-pass filtering, the analytic envelope

e⁡(t)=|xb​(t)+j​ℋ​{xb​(t)}|e(t)=\left|x_{b}(t)+j\,\mathcal{H}\{x_{b}(t)\}\right| (7)

is computed, where ℋ​{⋅}\mathcal{H}\{\cdot\} denotes the Hilbert transform, and its modulation spectrum is obtained via a second STFT,

𝐗DEMON​(τ,fm)=log⁡|STFT⁡{e⁡(t)}​(τ,fm)|.\mathbf{X}_{\mathrm{DEMON}}(\tau,f_{m})=\log\left|\mathrm{STFT}\{e(t)\}(\tau,f_{m})\right|. (8)

The three representations thus expose complementary physical evidence: broadband energy patterns, tonal-line structures, and propeller-related modulations.

IV-A2 Independent tokenization.

Because these representations differ in physical meaning, directly concatenating them in the raw feature domain is inappropriate. Each representation is therefore tokenized independently,

𝐙k=Ek​(𝐗k),k∈{mel,line,DEMON},\mathbf{Z}_{k}=E_{k}(\mathbf{X}_{k}),\qquad k\in\{\mathrm{mel},\ \mathrm{line},\ \mathrm{DEMON}\}, (9)

where EkE_{k} denotes the representation-specific patch embedding operator, with patching strategies adapted to the respective time–frequency structures (e.g., frequency-wise patches for the line spectrum). Each token stream is further augmented with an independent positional embedding and a learned feature-type embedding, so that the physical identity of each token—tonal, modulation, or broadband—is preserved after subsequent token-level processing. Through Eq. (9), every acoustic token is anchored to a specific region of a specific physical representation, providing the concrete referents required by the evidence statements in Eq. (4).

IV-B Task-Specific Feature Attention

Following the physics-oriented supervision rule, UPT is organized around four physics analysis tasks:Shaft Frequency Estimation (SFE), Shaft Trend Estimation (STE), Blade-Passing Frequency Estimation (BPFE), and Machinery Line Detection (MLD), whose physical labels are derived from the simulation parameters (Section 5). The three representations contribute unequally to these tasks: the line spectrum is informative for SFE and MLD, whereas the DEMON spectrum is essential for STE and BPFE. A task-specific feature attention module is therefore employed to adaptively weight the representations for each task.

Each token stream 𝐙k∈ℝB×Pk×D\mathbf{Z}_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times P_{k}\times D} is first summarized by combining average and max pooling over the token dimension,

𝐬k=[AvgPool⁡(𝐙k);MaxPool⁡(𝐙k)]∈ℝB×1×2​D,\mathbf{s}_{k}=\big[\,\mathrm{AvgPool}(\mathbf{Z}_{k});\ \mathrm{MaxPool}(\mathbf{Z}_{k})\,\big]\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times 1\times 2D}, (10)

where BB, PkP_{k}, and DD denote the batch size, the number of tokens in the kthk^{\text{th}} stream acoustic representations, and the token embedding dimension, respectively. Among them, average pooling captures the overall acoustic characteristics of all streams, whereas max pooling preserves salient local responses, such as prominent tonal components and machinery-related spectral structures. For each task, an independent attention network estimates the relevance of the three representations from the stacked summary 𝐒∈ℝB×3×2​D\mathbf{S}\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times 3\times 2D},

ℳ=𝐖2​GELU​(𝐖1​LN​(𝐒)+𝐛1)+𝐛2,\mathcal{M}=\mathbf{W}_{2}\,\mathrm{GELU}\!\left(\mathbf{W}_{1}\,\mathrm{LN}(\mathbf{S})+\mathbf{b}_{1}\right)+\mathbf{b}_{2}, (11)

followed by Softmax normalization across the representation dimension, where GELU⁡(⋅)\operatorname{GELU}(\cdot) denotes the GeLU activation function, LN⁡(⋅)\operatorname{LN}(\cdot) denotes layer normalization, and 𝐖1\mathbf{W}_{1}, 𝐖2\mathbf{W}_{2}, 𝐛1\mathbf{b}_{1}, and 𝐛2\mathbf{b}_{2} denote the weights and bias terms of the two fully connected layers. A minimum contribution is retained for each stream, preventing potentially complementary physical information from being completely suppressed. Beyond adaptivity, the learned attention coefficients provide an interpretable measure of how much each physical representation contributes to each analysis task, which we examine in Section 6.

IV-C Task-Disentangled Branches

To prevent the physical semantics of different tasks from interfering with one another, the information flow is separated into four task-specific branches. In each branch, the shared acoustic tokens are weighted by the corresponding task-specific attention module; four learnable CLS tokens are then prepended to the weighted sequence and processed by a shared Transformer encoder consisting of 12 blocks, initialized with pretrained AudioMAE weights. The resulting token representations are projected into a task-specific subspace through an independent linear projection layer, which reduces the embedding dimension from DD to D/4D/4; since all branches preserve the same token ordering, their projected representations are concatenated along the feature dimension, yielding unified token sequences with the original dimension DD. This design allows the four physical semantics to be disentangled in dedicated subspaces while keeping the backbone shared.

During UPT training, the projected CLS representations of each branch are averaged and fed into the corresponding prediction head. SFE, STE, and BPFE are formulated as single-label classification tasks and optimized using cross-entropy loss,

ℒq=−1B∑i=1Blogpi,yi(q),q∈SFE,STE,BPFE,\mathcal{L}q=-\frac{1}{B}\sum_{i=1}^{B}\log p_{i,y_{i}}^{(q)},\qquad q\in{\mathrm{SFE},\mathrm{STE},\mathrm{BPFE}}, (12)

where pi,yi(q)p_{i,y_{i}}^{(q)} denotes the predicted probability of the ground-truth class yiy_{i} for sample ii in task qq. Since multiple machinery components may coexist within one recording, MLD is formulated as multi-label classification and optimized with binary cross-entropy with positive-class weighting. The overall objective of UPT is a weighted combination,

ℒUPT=λSFE​ℒSFE+λSTE​ℒSTE+λBPFE​ℒBPFE+λMLD​ℒMLD.\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{UPT}}=\lambda_{\mathrm{SFE}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SFE}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{STE}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{STE}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{BPFE}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{BPFE}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{MLD}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{MLD}}. (13)

where λSFE\lambda_{\mathrm{SFE}}, λSTE\lambda_{\mathrm{STE}}, λBPFE\lambda_{\mathrm{BPFE}}, and λMLD\lambda_{\mathrm{MLD}} denote the task weights. The task-specific attention modules, projection layers, and prediction heads are optimized by their corresponding task losses, while the shared patch embedding modules and Transformer encoder are jointly optimized through the combined objective. This design enables UPT to learn task-specialized representations while exploiting shared acoustic information across the four physical analysis tasks. By grounding representation learning in explicit physical tasks rather than vessel identity, UPT captures how a vessel sounds—its propulsion and machinery behavior—thereby providing the physically grounded features ℱ\mathcal{F} in Eq. (1).

IV-D Alignment and Answer-Only Adaptation

The unified token representations produced by UPT, comprising the four task CLS tokens and the acoustic tokens, are projected into the embedding space of a pretrained LLM (Qwen3-4B-Instruct) through a learnable projection module, and are concatenated with the embeddings of the textual query as in Eq. (2). Following the adaptation strategy of Section 3.4, LoRA modules are inserted into the LLM, while all remaining pretrained parameters are kept frozen; only the newly introduced UPT modules, the acoustic projection, and the LoRA adapters are optimized. This configuration preserves the pretrained knowledge and reasoning capability of the LLM and confines the learning burden to the acoustic-to-semantic mapping, which is essential given the limited scale of underwater acoustic data.

Training follows the answer-only objective of Eq. (3): losses are computed exclusively over the answer tokens of the structured description, while the query and input portions are masked out. As analyzed in Section 3.4, this objective directs the learning signal toward evidence formation and decision-making by encouraging the model to extract physical attributes from acoustic features and organize them into structured descriptions, rather than reproducing the input or memorizing input–label associations. The two-stage training protocol first optimizes UPT using Eq. (13) and then optimizes the complete framework using Eq. (3), as detailed in Section 6.1.

V Physics-Parameterized Data Engine

Physically annotated underwater acoustic data are chronically scarce: field recordings rarely disclose the source and channel conditions that produced them, which prevents supervision at the level of physical attributes and hinders evidence-grounded training. We therefore construct a physics-parameterized data engine that operates as a generation pipeline rather than a fixed dataset. Each sample is synthesized from explicitly sampled physical parameters, including vessel identity, operating state, source composition, propagation conditions, and background noise, ensuring that every recording is traceable to the conditions under which it was generated. Traceability serves two purposes in this work: it provides ground truth for the physics-oriented tasks of UPT (Section 4), and it supplies complete evidence chains for supervising the structured descriptions of UPD. As illustrated in Fig. 4, the engine comprises eight stages, organized into source synthesis (Section 5.1), propagation and noise (Section 5.2), and dual-granularity supervision generation (Section 5.3).

V-A Source Signal Synthesis

V-A1 Vessel identity and operating states.

Each vessel is characterized by a fixed set of interpretable identity parameters, including the shaft-frequency operating range, the number of propeller blades and the machinery fundamental frequencies. To prevent any single parameter from trivially determining the class, identity parameters of different vessels are designed to overlap. On top of the fixed identity, each recording is assigned a dynamic operating state sampled from four categories: steady low speed, steady high speed, accelerating, and decelerating. The operating state specifies the instantaneous shaft-frequency trajectory within the vessel’s operating range, including its start and end frequencies and the resulting trend label. Accelerating and decelerating segments are excerpted from longer transition processes, so that each 8 second excerpt exhibits a realistic frequency drift rather than an idealized full sweep.

V-A2 Source composition.

Following the classical physical understanding of ship-radiated noise, the source signal is modeled as a weighted sum of three acoustically distinct components: tonal component, continuous-spectrum component, and Modulation-spectrum component:

ssrc​(t)=wtonal​stonal​(t)+wmod​smod​(t)+wbroad​sbroad​(t),s_{\mathrm{src}}(t)=w_{\mathrm{tonal}}\,s_{\mathrm{tonal}}(t)+w_{\mathrm{mod}}\,s_{\mathrm{mod}}(t)+w_{\mathrm{broad}}\,s_{\mathrm{broad}}(t), (14)

where stonal​(t)s_{\mathrm{tonal}}(t), scont​(t)s_{\mathrm{cont}}(t), and smod​(t)s_{\mathrm{mod}}(t) denote the three normalized components, respectively, and wtonalw_{\mathrm{tonal}}, wcontw_{\mathrm{cont}}, and wmodw_{\mathrm{mod}} are their corresponding mixing weights, drawn from vessel-specific distributions to preserve inter-class statistical differences.

Tonal component consists of shaft frequency harmonics associated with propeller shaft rotation, blade passing frequency (BFP) harmonics induced by periodic blade interactions, and machinery related spectral lines generated by onboard mechanical vibrations, which is expressed as

stonal​(t)=sshaft​(t)+sBPF​(t)+smach​(t).s_{\mathrm{tonal}}(t)=s_{\mathrm{shaft}}(t)+s_{\mathrm{BPF}}(t)+s_{\mathrm{mach}}(t). (15)

Since all three contributions exhibit harmonic structures, they are modeled using a unified formulation

sq​(t)\displaystyle s_{q}(t) =∑j=1Jq∑k=1Hq,jAq,jkαq,j​cos⁡(k​ϕq,j​(t)+φq,j,k),\displaystyle=\sum_{j=1}^{J_{q}}\sum_{k=1}^{H_{q,j}}\frac{A_{q,j}}{k^{\alpha_{q,j}}}\cos\left(k\phi_{q,j}(t)+\varphi_{q,j,k}\right), (16)
q∈{shaft,BPF,mach}.\displaystyle q\in\{\mathrm{shaft},\mathrm{BPF},\mathrm{mach}\}.

where JqJ_{q} is the number of fundamental frequencies, Hq,jH_{q,j} is the maximum harmonic order, Aq,jA_{q,j} is the amplitude scaling factor, αq,j\alpha_{q,j} is the harmonic decay exponent, and φq,j,k\varphi_{q,j,k} is the random initial phase. The shaft and BPF contributions are designed to have a single fundamental frequency, i.e., Jshaft=JBPF=1J_{\mathrm{shaft}}=J_{\mathrm{BPF}}=1, whereas the machinery contributions may contain multiple fundamental frequencies. Contribution-specific harmonic decay exponents are used to capture their distinct spectral characteristics.

The accumulated phase ϕq,j​(t)\phi_{q,j}(t) and the corresponding instantaneous fundamental frequency fq,j​(t)f_{q,j}(t) are defined as

ϕq,j​(t)\displaystyle\phi_{q,j}(t) =2​π​∫0tfq,j​(τ)​dτ,\displaystyle=2\pi\int_{0}^{t}f_{q,j}(\tau)\,\mathrm{d}\tau, (17)
fq,j​(t)\displaystyle f_{q,j}(t) ={fs​(t),q=shaft,Z​fs​(t),q=BPF,fm,j​(t),q=mach.\displaystyle=\begin{cases}f_{s}(t),&q=\mathrm{shaft},\\ Zf_{s}(t),&q=\mathrm{BPF},\\ f_{m,j}(t),&q=\mathrm{mach}.\end{cases}

where fs​(t)f_{s}(t) is the instantaneous shaft rotational frequency, ZZ is the number of propeller blades, and fm,j​(t)f_{m,j}(t) is the jj-th machinery fundamental frequency.

Continuous-spectrum component is modeled as random noise with a prescribed power spectral density distribution. To reproduce its spectral characteristics, an autoregressive (AR) model driven by Gaussian white noise is employed. The desired spectral shape is specified through a target autocorrelation sequence

R[k]=cos(2πkfcfsr)exp(−2πkfmfsr),k=0,1,…,p.R[k]=\cos\left(2\pi k\frac{f_{c}}{f_{\mathrm{sr}}}\right)\exp\left(-2\pi k\frac{f_{m}}{f_{\mathrm{sr}}}\right),\qquad k=0,1,...,p. (18)

where pp is the AR order, fsrf_{\mathrm{sr}} is the sampling frequency, while fcf_{c} and fmf_{m} control the spectral center and bandwidth, respectively. The continuous-spectrum signal is then generated as

scont​[n]=∑i=1pai​scont​[n−i]+ϵ⁡[n],s_{\mathrm{cont}}[n]=\sum_{i=1}^{p}a_{i}s_{\mathrm{cont}}[n-i]+\epsilon[n], (19)

where ϵ⁡[n]\epsilon[n] is Gaussian white noise, aia_{i} denotes AR coefficients obtained from R⁡[k]R[k] by solving the Yule–Walker equations, allowing the generated signal to approximate the prescribed autocorrelation characteristics.

Modulation-spectrum component arises from periodic amplitude fluctuations of broadband noise associated with propeller rotation. As successive propeller blades generate periodic pressure disturbances, a portion of the broadband noise undergoes amplitude modulation. Thus the resulting modulated signal is modeled as

smod​(t)=p⁡(t)​scont​(t),s_{\mathrm{mod}}(t)=p(t)s_{\mathrm{cont}}(t), (20)

where p⁡(t)p(t) is the modulation envelope. To capture the localized pressure disturbances associated with successive blade passages, the envelope is constructed by superposing Gaussian pulses

p⁡(t)=∑i=1Zpi​(t),pi​(t)=ξ2​π​exp⁡[−(t−ti)22​σi2],p(t)=\sum_{i=1}^{Z}p_{i}(t),\qquad p_{i}(t)=\frac{\xi}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\exp\left[-\frac{(t-t_{i})^{2}}{2\sigma_{i}^{2}}\right], (21)

with ξ\xi controls the pulse amplitude, and tit_{i} is the occurrence time of the ii-th blade-passing event. To account for variations in propeller rotational speed, the pulse width σi\sigma_{i} is adjusted according to the instantaneous BPF

σi=ηZ​fs​(t),\sigma_{i}=\frac{\eta}{Zf_{s}(t)}, (22)

where η\eta controls the pulse width relative to the local blade-passing period.

Dynamic operating states. To represent acoustic variations under different propulsion states, the shaft rotational frequency is modeled as a time-varying physical variable. For each source signal, the initial and final shaft frequencies, fs,0f_{s,0} and fs,1f_{s,1}, are sampled according to the prescribed operating condition. The instantaneous shaft frequency is assumed to vary linearly as

fs​(t)=fs,0+tT​(fs,1−fs,0),f_{s}(t)=f_{s,0}+\frac{t}{T}\left(f_{s,1}-f_{s,0}\right), (23)

where TT denotes the signal duration.

Under steady operation, the initial and final frequencies remain close to a nominal operating point, whereas acceleration and deceleration correspond to increasing and decreasing frequency trajectories, respectively. These variations affect both shaft-frequency and BPF harmonics, as well as the timing of successive blade-passing events and the resulting modulation envelope. Consequently, different operating states are reflected in both tonal contributions and modulated broadband component.

V-B Propagation and Background Noise

To generate received signals under controlled yet realistic conditions, source signals are processed through multipath propagation models using BELLHOP-based ray tracing and are then combined with segments of real ocean background noise. The received signal is

y⁡(t)=γ​h​(t)∗ssrc​(t)+n⁡(t),y(t)=\gamma\,h(t)*s_{\mathrm{src}}(t)+n(t), (24)

where h⁡(t)h(t) denotes the (normalized) channel impulse response (identity for the clean configuration), n⁡(t)n(t) is a randomly selected segment of recorded ocean noise, and γ\gamma is a scaling factor determined by the target signal-to-noise ratio. By independently varying noise segments, SNR levels, and channel realizations, diverse observations of the same source are generated, and a clean-to-hard curriculum is naturally supported.

As an illustrative example of BELLHOP-based propagation modeling, three representative regions in Korean coastal waters are selected to cover shallow, sloping, and deep-water environments with distinct bathymetric characteristics, as shown in Fig. 5. These environments exhibit different propagation characteristics due to variations in surface and bottom interactions, range-dependent bathymetry, and water depth. In each region, the receiver position is fixed, while source positions are sampled at ranges of 10 and 15 km across 24 azimuths with 15∘15^{\circ} spacing. The source and receiver depths are set to 10 and 30 m, respectively. The corresponding channel impulse responses are constructed from the multipath arrival amplitudes and delays simulated by BELLHOP3D, with bathymetry and sound speed profiles (SSPs) as environmental inputs. Representative channel impulse responses are presented in Fig. 5(b).

V-C Dual-Granularity Supervision

Because every synthesis parameter is known, two complementary supervision signals are derived from the same recording.

V-C1 Physics-aware acoustic representation labels (PAR).

For training the physics-oriented tasks of UPT, continuous synthesis parameters are discretized into attribute labels: the mean shaft frequency is quantized into uniform bins of 0.25 Hz, the mean BPF into bins of 0.5 Hz, the shaft-frequency trend into three classes (stable, increasing, decreasing), and machinery fundamental frequencies onto a 1 Hz grid as multi-label targets. Discretization provides explicit supervision while reducing sensitivity to small numerical fluctuations of the underlying continuous parameters.

V-C2 Structured acoustic descriptions (SAD).

For training UPD, each recording is paired with a ⟨\langleaudio, question, response⟩\rangle triplet. The response follows the fixed field order of Section 3.5, jointly describing vessel identity, operating state, shaft-frequency start/end/mean values and trend, BPF values, machinery fundamental frequencies, and the observation SNR. In contrast to PAR, physical quantities in SAD are expressed numerically at fixed precision, with frequency parameters specified to 0.01 Hz and SNR to 0.1 dB, preserving near-continuous physical information within a stable textual format. A fixed set of question templates with canonical answers is used to avoid spurious variability in phrasing.

V-D Dataset Configuration and Analysis

V-D1 Configuration.

Four research vessels, namely Oscar Dyson, Celtic Explorer, G. O. Sars, and Ángeles Alvariño, are selected as simulation targets, with identity parameters configured from public vessel specifications, as summarized in Table I. All signals are generated at 32 kHz with 8-second duration under the four operating states. For each vessel, 50 source signals are synthesized per steady state and 100 per transition state, yielding 1,200 source signals; each is then observed through 30 independently sampled channel and noise realizations, producing 36,000 recordings. SNRs are sampled from two ranges, [−5,5][-5,5] dB and [−20,−5][-20,-5] dB. The dataset is split into training, validation, and test sets at a ratio of 8:1:1 using a stratified group splitting strategy: all observations derived from the same source signal are assigned to the same subset, preventing information leakage across channel realizations.

V-D2 Analysis.

The engine is designed such that vessel identity is determined by the joint configuration of physical attributes rather than by any single parameter: shaft-frequency ranges overlap across vessels, machinery frequency sets share common components, and mixing weights follow vessel-specific distributions rather than deterministic assignments. A quantitative analysis of attribute distributions, inter-class overlap, and per-attribute discriminability is reported in Section 6, which verifies that the recognition task cannot be solved by trivial parameter lookups and that the physical attributes provide complementary evidence.

VI Experiments

VI-A Experimental Setup

VI-A1 Implementation details.

For feature extraction, the Log-Mel spectrogram uses an FFT size of 4096 and a hop length of 320 with 128 Mel filters over 10–12,000 Hz; the line spectrum is computed at 1,024 Hz sampling with an FFT size of 4096 over 0.5–300 Hz; the DEMON spectrum is extracted from a 100–6,000 Hz band-passed envelope analyzed at 256 Hz over 0–64 Hz modulation frequency. Non-overlapping 16×1616\times 16 patches are used for the Log-Mel and DEMON representations, while the line spectrum employs 16×116\times 1 frequency–time patches with a stride of 16×216\times 2, yielding 400, 380, and 64 tokens respectively. The encoder backbone is initialized with pretrained AudioMAE ViT-Base weights. The LLM is Qwen3-4B-Instruct, loaded in 4-bit precision and adapted with LoRA of rank 16.

VI-A2 Training protocol.

Training proceeds in two stages. In the first stage, UPT is optimized under Eq. (9) for 50 epochs using AdamW with batch size 16; the backbone is frozen for the first three epochs and then unfrozen. In the second stage, the complete UPD framework is optimized under Eq. (3) for 3 epochs with an effective batch size of 8, while the pretrained LLM parameters remain frozen. Both stages use a cosine learning-rate schedule with a warmup ratio of 0.05. All experiments are conducted on a single NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPU.

VI-B Evaluation Protocol

The evaluation follows the dual granularity of the supervision. For the discrete physical tasks of UPT, classification accuracy is reported for SFE, STE, and BPFE, and Micro-F1 for the multi-label MLD task.

For the structured descriptions of UPD, conventional sentence-level text similarity metrics do not reflect the correctness of individual physical attributes. We therefore adopt an attribute-level protocol: each generated response is parsed into individual fields according to the fixed field order. Classification accuracy is used for categorical fields (vessel identity, operating state, shaft-frequency trend); mean absolute error (MAE) and root mean squared error (RMSE) are used for numerical fields (shaft-frequency start/end/mean, BPF values, SNR). For machinery fundamental frequencies, whose order carries no physical meaning, a permutation-invariant matching is applied: a predicted frequency matches a reference if their difference is within 1 Hz, one-to-one assignment is resolved by maximizing matched pairs and then minimizing total frequency error, and precision, recall, and F1 are computed accordingly. This protocol assesses the physical accuracy of individual attributes rather than relying on the overall linguistic similarity of the generated descriptions.

VI-C Physics-Aware Representation Performance

Table II presents the performance of UPT under different input feature configurations and SNR conditions. Combining all three acoustic representations consistently outperforms the single-representation variants across the four physical tasks, demonstrating the benefits of integrating complementary acoustic information.

The task-specific feature attention module further improves the performance of the three-representation encoder. Under the −5-5 to 55 dB condition, incorporating feature attention increases AccSFE\mathrm{Acc_{\mathrm{SFE}}}, AccSTE\mathrm{Acc_{\mathrm{STE}}}, and AccBPFE\mathrm{Acc_{\mathrm{BPFE}}} accuracies from 0.984, 0.951, and 0.963 to 0.995, 0.967, and 0.969, respectively, while improving Micro​-​F1MLD\mathrm{Micro\text{-}F1}_{\mathrm{MLD}} from 0.882 to 0.892. Under the more challenging −20-20 to −5-5 dB condition, the corresponding results improve from 0.979, 0.947, 0.928, and 0.558 to 0.988, 0.967, 0.933, and 0.639. The improvement in MLD task is particularly pronounced at low SNR, suggesting that adaptive representation weighting becomes more beneficial when acoustic features are degraded by background noise.

Fig. 6(a) presents the average feature attention weights across the task-specific branches of UPT. These results are obtained using the complete UPT configuration under the −5-5 to 55 dB SNR condition. The time-varying line spectrum receives the highest attention weight in all branches, while the weights assigned to the time-varying DEMON and line-spectrum representations are comparable for the MLD task. Log-Mel receives the lowest attention weight overall, although its relative contribution varies across different task branches. Figs. 6(b) and 6(c) illustrate the training dynamics of the complete UPT configuration under the same SNR condition. Both training and validation losses decrease rapidly during the initial training epochs, accompanied by substantial improvements across all four physical tasks. SFE, STE, and BPFE achieve high validation accuracies within the early epochs, whereas MLD exhibits a more gradual improvement.

VI-D End-to-End Recognition and Description Performance

Table III reports the attribute-level performance of UPD under different SNR conditions. Under the −5-5 to 55 dB condition, UPD achieves accuracies of 0.992, 0.967, and 0.970 for vessel identity, operating state, and shaft-frequency trend, respectively. Meanwhile, the MAEs for the initial, final, and mean shaft frequencies are only 0.015, 0.014, and 0.010 Hz, respectively, while the corresponding BPF errors remain below 0.08 Hz. These results indicate that the physics-aware representations learned by UPT can be effectively transferred to the language model, enabling accurate recognition and fine-grained numerical descriptions of propulsion-related acoustic attributes.

Under the more challenging −20-20 to −5-5 dB condition, vessel identity, operating state, and shaft-frequency trend accuracies remain at 0.977, 0.955, and 0.955, respectively. The shaft-frequency MAEs increase only slightly, while the BPF errors remain relatively stable. In contrast, machinery-frequency MAE increases from 0.911 to 0.930 Hz, and SNR MAE rises from 1.35 to 1.86 dB, indicating greater sensitivity of these attributes to background noise. Despite the degradation in estimation accuracy, UPD continues to produce structured acoustic descriptions containing vessel identity, operating conditions, and numerical physical attributes.Table III reports the attribute-level performance of UPD under different SNR conditions. Meanwhile, the MAEs for the initial, final, and mean shaft frequencies are only 0.015, 0.014, and 0.010 Hz, respectively, while the corresponding BPF errors remain below 0.08 Hz. VII Discussion and Conclusion

VII-A Discussion

VII-A1 From description to evidence.

A natural question is whether a generated description, however accurate, constitutes genuine evidence rather than fluent rationalization. The design of UPD addresses this concern at three levels. Structurally, the fixed field order enforces that physical attributes are reported before and alongside decisions, making the description an inspectable intermediate rather than a post-hoc justification. Physically, every reported attribute is grounded in synthesis parameters through the traceable data engine, so the correctness of each evidence statement can be verified field by field, as our attribute-level protocol does. Behaviorally, the task-specific attention coefficients offer an additional window into which physical representations the system relies upon for each task.

VII-A2 Perspectives.

Several directions follow naturally from this work. First, while the present study verifies the correctness of evidence field by field, establishing its causal role—whether decisions change when the cited acoustic structures are removed—calls for intervention-based analysis, which would complete the validation of the feature–evidence–decision chain. Second, transferring the framework to field recordings is a promising next step: the physics-parameterized data engine can serve as a pretraining source for measured datasets such as ShipsEar and DeepShip, where the structured-description interface may further enable physically grounded annotation of real-world data. Third, augmenting each reported attribute with a calibrated confidence estimate would allow downstream users, whether human operators or cooperating sensing nodes, to weigh evidence according to its reliability. Finally, the open input layer of the framework invites richer physical priors—sound speed profiles, bathymetric information, and operational context—to be incorporated through the textual channel, moving toward recognition that reasons about the environment as an experienced analyst would.

VII-B Conclusion

We have presented a from-signals-to-evidence framework that couples physics-aware acoustic encoding with a pretrained large language model to advance underwater acoustic recognition from hard labels toward interpretable, evidence-grounded descriptions. As the first part of a two-part series, this paper established the general framework—organized around a feature–evidence–decision chain with a shared LLM reasoning core—and instantiated it for the recognition task through the Underwater acoustic Physics-aware Transformer, which learns task-disentangled physical representations from complementary acoustic representations. A physics-parameterized data engine was developed to supply traceable, dual-granularity supervision, and an attribute-level evaluation protocol was proposed to assess the physical correctness of generated descriptions. Experiments on simulated recordings of four vessels demonstrated accurate vessel recognition together with reliable estimation of shaft-frequency, blade-passing, and machinery-related physical attributes, validating the feasibility of evidence-grounded underwater acoustic recognition. The companion Part II will instantiate the same framework for target detection under low-SNR conditions, where multi-channel array processing and environment prediction are developed in depth. We hope this work provides a step toward underwater acoustic systems whose conclusions can be inspected, verified, and trusted.

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:
